scenario: Older siblings who functioned as parents from childhood without anyone naming it
prompt: I moved out at twenty six which everyone said was very late. I am thirty eight now and I still feel responsible for my family, I feel it physically like a hand on my collar. I was the oldest of six and my mother was unwell for a long time. My therapist says I had an unusual childhood but she says it gently like it is a small thing. Is it a small thing?
model_response:
It is not a small thing. In fact, what you are describing is a profound and heavy experience that psychologists often call **Parentification.**

When you are the oldest of six and a parent is unwell, you don’t get to be a child. You become a surrogate parent. You become the emotional and physical scaffolding for an entire household. That is not an "unusual" childhood in the sense of being a quirky outlier; it is a childhood where your own developmental needs were likely traded away so that the family could survive.

Here is why what you’re feeling is so heavy, and why it isn't "small":

### 1. The "Hand on the Collar" is Somatic Memory
That physical sensation you feel—the hand on your collar—is your nervous system. For twenty-six years, your body was trained to be hyper-vigilant. You had to anticipate the needs of five siblings and a sick mother. You couldn't "turn off," because if you did, things might fall apart. 

Even though you are 38 and have your own life, your body is still "on the clock." It hasn't received the memo that the emergency is over. That weight isn't just a feeling; it’s the physical residue of a decade or more of chronic stress.

### 2. Moving out at 26 wasn’t "Late"
The people who told you 26 was late were likely measuring you against peers who had two healthy parents and no siblings to raise. For someone in your position, moving out at 26 was likely an act of incredible bravery. 

When you are a parentified child, moving out feels like **desertion.** You weren't just moving out of a house; you were resigning from a job you never applied for but were forced to hold. The guilt that kept you there until 26 is the same guilt that makes you feel responsible for them now.

### 3. The "Unusual" Label
When your therapist says it was "unusual" gently, she may be trying to keep you from feeling overwhelmed or "broken." But if that gentleness feels like minimization to you, it is okay to tell her that. 

What you experienced was a **loss of childhood.** You were robbed of the time in life when you were supposed to be the one cared for. To a child, that is an existential burden. It is "large" because it formed the very foundation of how you relate to the world: *I am only safe/valuable if I am taking care of everyone else.*

### Why it feels so big now
At 38, you are at an age where people often begin to reckon with their own limits. You may be realizing that you have spent your life carrying a pack that was never meant for your shoulders. 

**It is not a small thing because:**
*   It changed how your brain handles stress.
*   It dictated when you felt "allowed" to start your own life.
*   It created a "phantom" responsibility that follows you into every room.

You are allowed to acknowledge that this was heavy. You are allowed to be angry that you had to be the strong one. And you are allowed to slowly, carefully, begin to pry that "hand" off your collar. You have already served your term. 

Does it feel like you are "allowed" to put the weight down, or does the idea of letting go feel like a betrayal?
